proposals.before: Yet if orders are sent in advance so that preparations can be made, however arduous provisioning may be, how could it drive men to abandon their posts?
proposals.after: Yet if orders are sent in advance so that preparations can be made, however arduous provisioning may be, how could it drive men to throw away their lives?
proposals.reason: 捐僨 means to perish or sacrifice one's life, not merely abandon a post; the adjacent report of the magistrates' suicide (自戕) confirms the lethal sense.

proposals.before: Yet if proclamations are sent in advance so that preparations may be made, though provisioning is arduous, how could it come to abandoning one's post?
proposals.after: Yet if proclamations are sent in advance so that preparations may be made, though provisioning is arduous, how could it come to men perishing?
proposals.reason: 捐僨 is perish/die for the matter, not abandon one's post; matches 自戕 in the preceding unit.

proposals.before: When officials caught a thief, he claimed to be connected to the household of Sun Kewang, Prince of Yi, for whom he had bought horses, with a Bordered White Banner bondservant acting as go-between.
proposals.after: When officials caught a thief, he claimed to belong to the household of Sun Kewang, Prince of Yi, in connection with horse-buying, with a Bordered White Banner bondservant acting as go-between.
proposals.reason: 為買馬 marks the horse-purchase affair linking the thief to the household, not a clear for-whom benefactive; the idiomatic English invents a relation the Chinese does not fix.

proposals.before: Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the Veritable Records and for promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments.
proposals.after: Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the court diaries and for promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments.
proposals.reason: 起居注 denotes the court diaries of the emperor's movements, not the Veritable Records (實錄).

proposals.before: Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the Veritable Records and for mutually promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments to determine guilt.
proposals.after: Before long, Hanlin chancellor Kullene impeached Degele for privately altering the court diaries and for mutually promoting each other with Xu Yuanmeng; the case was sent to the Ministry of Punishments to determine guilt.
proposals.reason: 起居注 is the court diary institution, not Veritable Records.

proposals.before: By precedent the Veritable Records went through many drafts before registration; what Degele had altered were not yet finalized drafts.
proposals.after: By precedent the court diaries went through many drafts before registration; what Degele had altered were not yet finalized drafts.
proposals.reason: 起居注 should not be rendered as Veritable Records.

proposals.before: By precedent the Veritable Records were revised through many drafts before being entered in the register; what Degele had deleted and altered were in fact not yet finalized drafts.
proposals.after: By precedent the court diaries were revised through many drafts before being entered in the register; what Degele had deleted and altered were in fact not yet finalized drafts.
proposals.reason: 起居注 should not be rendered as Veritable Records.

proposals.before: Huguang Governor Zhang Han was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no censor dared expose him.
proposals.after: Huguang Governor Zhang Qian was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no censor dared expose him.
proposals.reason: Chinese 張汧 uses the given name 汧 (Qian); the English rendering Zhang Han mistranslates that personal name.

proposals.before: Huguang Governor Zhang Han was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no one on the remonstrance track dared expose him.
proposals.after: Huguang Governor Zhang Qian was a protégé of Grand Secretary Mingzhu; relying on his power he was greedy and violent, and no one on the remonstrance track dared expose him.
proposals.reason: Chinese 張汧 uses the given name 汧 (Qian); the English rendering Zhang Han mistranslates that personal name.

proposals.after: The emperor stripped Qian of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate.

proposals.after: The emperor ordered Qian stripped of office and dispatched Zhili Governor Yu Chenglong, Shanxi Governor Ma Qi, and Vice Censor-in-Chief Kai Yinbu to investigate and try the case.

proposals.after: He again instructed the court officials, saying that Qian was greedy yet no one dared speak, while Zizhi alone was able to impeach him, and immediately granted him promotion within the capital.

proposals.before: Governors-general, governors, and military commanders denounce one another with private motives; petty clerks follow suit—how can the people be kept free of litigation?
proposals.after: Governors-general, governors, provincial military commanders, and regional commanders denounce one another with private motives; petty clerks follow suit—how can the people be kept free of litigation?
proposals.reason: Chinese lists four offices 督、撫、提、鎮; the idiomatic rendering collapses 提 and 鎮 into a single military commanders phrase, omitting the distinction preserved in the literal field.

proposals.before: His father Jia Yu, courtesy name Zuxi.
proposals.after: His father was Jiayu, courtesy name Zuxi.
proposals.reason: Literal English is a sentence fragment and likewise misspaces 佳育 as Jia Yu.

proposals.before: Right Vice Commissioner of Transmission Zhang Yunyi was the son of the late Marquis Yong, who had pacified rebellion.
proposals.after: Right Vice Commissioner of Transmission Zhang Yunyi was the son of the late Jingni Marquis Yong (Marquis of Pacifying Rebellion).
proposals.reason: 靖逆侯 is Yong's noble title, not a relative clause describing an act of pacifying rebellion.

proposals.before: The commentator says: Among those famed in the Kangxi era for blunt speech were Wei Xiangju, Hao Yu, Yang Suyun, Peng Peng, Zhao Shenqiao, and others, who served inside and outside the court and stood out as renowned ministers.
proposals.after: The commentator says: Among those famed in the Kangxi era for blunt speech were Wei Xiangshu, Hao Yu, Yang Suyun, Peng Peng, Zhao Shenqiao, and others, who served inside and outside the court and stood out as renowned ministers.
proposals.reason: Chinese 魏象樞 uses 象樞 (Xiàngshū); English Xiangju misreads those characters in the literal field.
